guide.summary: Unit 8 covers pollution of water and land and its effects on ecosystems and human health: point and nonpoint sources, oil spills, endocrine disruptors, wetlands, eutrophication, thermal pollution, persistent organic pollutants, bioaccumulation and biomagnification, solid waste and its reduction, sewage treatment, toxicology (LD50, dose-response), and infectious diseases.

sections.heading: Sources and aquatic impacts
sections.body: Point sources come from a single identifiable location (a factory pipe, a sewage outfall); nonpoint sources are diffuse (farm runoff, urban storm water) and harder to regulate. Oil spills coat feathers and fur, reducing insulation, and are toxic when ingested. Coral reefs are harmed by sediment, warming, and acidification. Wetlands and mangroves filter pollutants, reduce flooding, and protect coastlines; they are lost to development, agriculture, and dams. Indicator species (e.g., mayfly and stonefly larvae) reveal water quality: their presence means clean, well-oxygenated water.

sections.heading: Eutrophication and thermal pollution
sections.body: Eutrophication sequence: excess nitrogen and phosphorus (fertilizer, sewage, detergents) → algal bloom → algae block light and die → decomposers break down dead algae, using up dissolved oxygen → hypoxic dead zones and fish kills. The oxygen crash is caused by decomposition, not by the living algae. Oligotrophic waters are nutrient-poor and clear; eutrophic waters are nutrient-rich. Downstream of a sewage outfall, dissolved oxygen sags to a minimum some distance away (where decomposition peaks) and then recovers. Thermal pollution (warm water from power plants) lowers dissolved oxygen, raises organisms' metabolic oxygen demand, and causes thermal shock.

sections.heading: Toxins, POPs, and biomagnification
sections.body: Endocrine disruptors (e.g., atrazine, BPA, some phthalates) mimic or block hormones, causing reproductive and developmental effects such as feminization of male frogs. Persistent organic pollutants (DDT, PCBs, dioxins) are fat-soluble, resist breakdown, and travel long distances. Bioaccumulation is buildup within an organism over its lifetime; biomagnification is increasing concentration at higher trophic levels because predators eat many contaminated prey. Mercury from coal combustion becomes methylmercury in water, biomagnifies in fish, and causes neurological damage. DDT thinned eggshells in birds of prey.

sections.heading: Solid waste and sewage
sections.body: Sanitary landfills use clay and plastic liners, leachate collection systems, daily soil cover, and methane capture; problems include leachate contaminating groundwater and methane emissions. Incineration reduces volume but produces air pollution and toxic ash. Ocean dumping and plastics cause entanglement and ingestion. Waste reduction priority: reduce > reuse > recycle; composting diverts food and yard waste; e-waste contains heavy metals. Sewage treatment: primary (physical: screens and settling tanks remove solids), secondary (biological: bacteria break down organic matter, reducing biochemical oxygen demand), tertiary (chemical/ecological: removes nitrogen and phosphorus), then disinfection (chlorine, UV, or ozone). Combined sewer systems can overflow during heavy rain, releasing untreated sewage.

sections.heading: Toxicology and health
sections.body: LD50 is the dose that kills 50% of a test population, usually in mg per kg body mass; a lower LD50 means a more toxic substance. A dose-response curve plots effect against dose; a threshold is the dose below which no effect is seen; ED50 is the dose producing an effect in 50%. Toxicity data from animal studies may not translate perfectly to humans. Health hazards include respiratory problems from smog, lead poisoning, and mercury. Infectious diseases spread through contaminated water (cholera, dysentery), vectors (malaria, Zika and dengue by mosquitoes, Lyme disease by ticks), and are worsened by poverty, poor sanitation, crowding, and climate change expanding vector ranges.

sections.heading: Worked example: LD50 and dose-response
sections.body: In a toxicology study, the LD50 is the dose that kills 50% of a test population; a lower LD50 means a more toxic substance. If substance A has an LD50 of 5 mg/kg and substance B has 500 mg/kg, substance A is 100 times more toxic by this measure. Dose-response curves show the relationship between exposure and effect, and the threshold is the dose below which no effect is observed.

sections.heading: Biomagnification
sections.body: Persistent, fat-soluble pollutants such as DDT and mercury accumulate in organisms (bioaccumulation) and increase in concentration at higher trophic levels (biomagnification). DDT caused eggshell thinning in birds of prey such as bald eagles, which recovered after DDT was banned in the United States in 1972.

sections.heading: Common errors
sections.body: Students confuse bioaccumulation (within an organism) with biomagnification (up a food chain).

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know point and nonpoint sources, eutrophication, hypoxia, dead zones, thermal pollution, persistent organic pollutants, bioaccumulation, biomagnification, LD50, sanitary landfills, and wastewater treatment.

keyTakeaways: Point vs. nonpoint: one pipe vs. diffuse runoff.
Eutrophication's oxygen crash comes from decomposers.
Biomagnification: concentration rises up the food chain.
Sewage: primary physical, secondary biological, tertiary nutrients.
Landfills: liners, leachate collection, methane capture.
commonMistakes: Saying algae consume the oxygen during eutrophication.
Thinking a higher LD50 means more toxic.
Calling farm runoff a point source.
Assuming warm water holds more oxygen.
examTips: Put the eutrophication steps in order with cause and effect.
Biomagnification calculations compare concentrations across levels (multiply or divide).
LD50 problems convert mg/kg to a total dose for a given body mass.
Landfill FRQs often include volume and lifespan calculations.
guide.cramSheet:
**Sources:** point (pipe) · nonpoint (runoff)

**Eutrophication:** N, P → bloom → die-off → decomposers use O₂ → dead zone

**Thermal:** warm water → ↓ DO, ↑ metabolism

**Toxins:** endocrine disruptors · POPs fat-soluble, persistent · bioaccumulation (one organism) · biomagnification (food chain)

**Waste:** reduce > reuse > recycle · landfill liner, leachate, methane

**Sewage:** primary settle · secondary bacteria (↓ BOD) · tertiary N, P · disinfect

**Tox:** LD50 lower = more toxic · threshold · total dose = LD50 × body mass

Wastewater discharged from a paper mill's outflow pipe
Oil washed from city streets during rain
Sediment from logging roads across a forest

choices.text: methylmercury, which biomagnifies and damages the developing nervous system

practice.stimulus: Dissolved oxygen was measured at points along a river: 9 mg/L just above a sewage outfall, 7 mg/L at the outfall, 3 mg/L 10 km downstream, 6 mg/L at 25 km, and 8.5 mg/L at 40 km.
practice.stem: Which explanation best accounts for the lowest value occurring 10 km downstream rather than at the outfall?

choices.text: The water is warmer at 40 km.
Algae at the outfall produce extra oxygen.
Bacterial decomposition of organic matter in the sewage increases as bacteria multiply, so oxygen demand peaks downstream before the river reaerates.
Fish are more abundant at 10 km and consume the oxygen.

practice.explanation: This is the classic oxygen-sag curve: BOD-driven decomposition takes time and distance to peak.

choices.text: Recycling still requires energy for collection and processing, while reducing avoids extraction, manufacturing, and disposal entirely.

practice.frqType: Q3 Analyze an Environmental Problem and Propose a Solution Doing Calculations
practice.prompt: A town of 40,000 people generates an average of 2.0 kg of municipal solid waste per person per day, all sent to a new sanitary landfill. The landfill has a capacity of 2.0 × 10⁶ m³, and compacted waste has a density of 500 kg/m³. Assume 365 days per year.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the mass of waste, in kg, the town generates per year. Show your work.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the volume, in m³, this waste occupies per year. Show your work.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate how many years until the landfill is full. Show your work.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: The town begins a recycling and composting program that diverts 30% of its waste. Calculate the new landfill lifespan. Show your work.

parts.label: e
parts.prompt: Describe how leachate forms and explain how the landfill design prevents it from contaminating groundwater.

parts.label: f
parts.prompt: Explain one environmental benefit of capturing methane from the landfill.

parts.label: g
parts.prompt: Propose one waste reduction strategy (other than recycling) and explain how it reduces the volume of waste sent to the landfill.

rubric.description: Rainwater percolates through waste, dissolving and carrying chemicals, metals, and organic compounds.
A compacted clay and plastic liner blocks the liquid, and a pipe system collects leachate for treatment.
Methane is a potent greenhouse gas; capturing and burning it reduces climate warming and can generate electricity in place of fossil fuels (also reduces explosion risk).
E.g., composting food and yard waste, banning single-use plastics, pay-as-you-throw pricing, reusable containers.
Explains how the strategy keeps a specific portion of waste out of the landfill.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) 40,000 people × 2.0 kg/person/day × 365 days/yr = 2.92 × 10⁷ kg per year.

(b) 2.92 × 10⁷ kg ÷ 500 kg/m³ = 5.84 × 10⁴ m³ per year.

(c) 2.0 × 10⁶ m³ ÷ 5.84 × 10⁴ m³/yr ≈ 34 years.

(d) New annual volume = 5.84 × 10⁴ × 0.70 = 4.09 × 10⁴ m³/yr. 2.0 × 10⁶ ÷ 4.09 × 10⁴ ≈ 49 years.

(e) As rain falls on the landfill, water trickles through the waste and dissolves chemicals, heavy metals, and decomposing organic matter, forming leachate. A compacted clay layer beneath a thick plastic liner stops leachate from seeping into the ground, and perforated pipes above the liner collect it so it can be pumped to a treatment facility.

(f) Methane is a greenhouse gas many times more potent than CO₂. Capturing it and burning it to generate electricity prevents its release and replaces some fossil fuel use.

(g) Start a curbside food-waste composting program. Food and yard waste make up a large share of household trash; composting them turns that material into soil amendment instead of sending it to the landfill.
